cur:monumental-san-clemente-christ-angel.summary: A bearded Christ, frontal and haloed, sits between two winged archangels in court dress, raising his right hand in blessing against a deep blue ground. The scene is usually interpreted as the 'particular judgement' of an individual soul presented to Christ, a rare theme in early medieval painting.
facts: Apart from Santa Maria Antiqua, the lower basilica of San Clemente holds the largest collection of early medieval wall paintings in Rome; the church was buried beneath the new basilica built around 1099–1120.
cur:monumental-san-clemente-christ-angel.notes: The image is a small, enhanced reproduction; the full scene includes figures not visible here.

cur:objects-notger-gospels-ivory.summary: In the upper part of this ivory plaque Christ sits in majesty in a mandorla, blessing, surrounded by the four evangelist symbols; below, Bishop Notger of Liège kneels in prayer before a small church building. The plaque, framed by later Mosan enamels and gilded lobes, covers a gospel book that belonged to the collegiate church of St John the Evangelist in Liège. It is a moving image of a bishop entrusting himself and his foundation to Christ.
facts: According to the Grand Curtius label, the gospel book belonged until the early 18th century to the collegiate church of Saint-Jean-l'Évangéliste in Liège, founded by Bishop Notger; the manuscript itself was written and illuminated at Reims around 930.

Notker (Notger) was bishop of Liège from 972 to 1008 and the city's first prince-bishop; Wikipedia notes that he founded St John's on the model of Aachen and appears to have commissioned this Evangeliary.
